pinterest.title: Merguez Biryani with Caramelised Onions — French-Pakistani Fusion
pinterest.description: Merguez biryani takes spiced North African lamb sausage and layers it through long-grain basmati with deep-mahogany caramelised onions. Dum-cooked until the steam does its quiet work. This is French-Pakistani fusion that actually earns its place at the table — bold, aromatic, and worth every minute of the caramelising. Recipe at mubashirr.com

instagram.caption:
Some fusions feel forced. This one felt inevitable.

Merguez is a North African sausage that found a home in French butcher shops and Parisian street markets. Biryani is the dish every South Asian cook treats as a personal statement. Put them together and you get something that shouldn't work on paper but absolutely does in the pot.

The merguez brings harissa heat, cumin, and fennel — spices that speak the same language as a Pakistani masala, just with a different accent. The caramelised onions take longer than you want them to. That's the point. Patience turns them mahogany, sticky, almost jammy, and they dissolve into the rice in a way that no shortcut produces.

Dum cooking seals everything under a tight lid. The steam circulates, the flavours knit together, and what comes out is a biryani that feels both familiar and genuinely new.

The full recipe is linked in bio. Make it on a weekend when you can give the onions the time they need.

email.subject: Biryani meets the French butcher shop
email.preheader: Merguez, basmati, and the caramelised onions you can't rush.
email.body_html:
There is a particular kind of cooking problem I find interesting: take two things with strong identities and see whether they can share a pot without one erasing the other.

Merguez biryani is my answer to that problem.

Merguez is a sausage with North African roots and a long, comfortable life in French charcuterie. It carries harissa, cumin, and fennel — a spice profile that turns out to speak fluent biryani without needing translation. Layered through long-grain basmati and sealed under a dum lid, it produces rice that is fragrant, faintly smoky, and genuinely surprising even when you already know what is in it.

The caramelised onions are non-negotiable and non-rushable. They take the better part of an hour over low heat to reach the deep mahogany colour that makes them worth adding. Pull them too early and they taste like onions. Give them the time and they dissolve into the rice as something closer to a condiment — sweet, slightly bitter at the edges, and essential.

This is not fusion for the sake of novelty. It is two culinary traditions that happen to share enough common ground that the result feels less like an experiment and more like something that should have existed already.

The full recipe, with timings and technique notes for both the dum seal and the sausage preparation, is on the site.

Read the recipe: Merguez Biryani with Caramelised Onions

linkedin.body:
I have been thinking about what makes a fusion recipe worth publishing versus what makes it a gimmick.

The test I keep returning to: do the two elements actually need each other, or is one just a costume the other is wearing?

Merguez biryani passes that test.

Merguez carries harissa, cumin, and fennel. Those spices are not exotic additions to a biryani context — they are close relatives of the masala the rice is already expecting. The sausage format also solves a real cooking problem: it keeps the meat moist and self-contained through the dum process, which is longer and more enclosed than most Western braises.

The French technique that matters here is not anything elaborate. It is patience with the caramelised onions. French classical cooking has always treated the low, slow caramelisation of alliums as foundational rather than optional. Pakistani biryani does too, but it is often where home cooks reach for shortcuts. The mahogany onions in this recipe are what carry the sweetness that balances the sausage heat. Cut that step short and the whole dish is flatter for it.

What I find genuinely interesting about cooking across traditions is not the novelty. It is that the same instincts — layering, patience, building depth before combining — show up independently in kitchens that never spoke to each other.

Full recipe and technique notes: https://mubashirr.com/merguez-biryani-caramelised-onions/

tweets: Merguez biryani shouldn't work. North African sausage, Pakistani rice technique, French caramelised onions. And yet it is one of the most coherent things I have cooked this year. Here is why it holds together.

Merguez carries harissa, cumin, fennel. Those are not foreign flavours to a biryani masala — they are cousins. The sausage casing also keeps the meat moist through the dum seal in a way loose ground meat rarely does.

The caramelised onions are the French contribution. Not a technique borrowed for aesthetics — they are doing real work. An hour over low heat turns them mahogany and slightly jammy. They provide the sweetness that keeps the sausage heat from running away with the dish.

Dum cooking is the final piece. Tight lid, low heat, steam circulating through the layers. The rice absorbs the merguez fat and the onion sweetness and comes out as something that tastes like it was always supposed to exist.
Full recipe with timing and technique notes here: https://mubashirr.com/merguez-biryani-caramelised-onions/ — worth making on a weekend when you can give the onions the time they need.

The cumin and fennel in merguez speak the same language as a biryani masala. The dum seal does the rest. This is one of those recipes where the technique matters as much as the ingredients, and the full breakdown is on the site.
